title: Wang Yangming: The Unity of Knowledge and Action
excerpt: Excerpted from Xu Baoyun's The Sage of the Mind: Wang Yangming

inline.s: Excerpted from Xu Baoyun's The Sage of the Mind: Wang Yangming
Wang Shouren
(Wang Yangming)
, after his enlightenment at Longchang, founded the doctrine of “the unity of knowledge and action,” and in the city of Beijing he gathered many disciples and lectured widely on his learning
His fame grew ever greater, and his teaching of “the unity of knowledge and action” gradually spread throughout the land
. His old friend

Gu Lin, of course, had also heard of it and had long wanted to find an occasion to discuss learning with Wang Shouren at length. But, not being master of his own time, he never had a chance to meet him. Now, having come to the capital on business, Gu Lin seized the opportunity to call on Wang Shouren, meet him, and renew their old friendship.
[Wang Shouren (1472–1529
)], childhood name Yun, courtesy name Bo'an, sobriquet Yangming, was a native of Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang (present-day Yuyao, Ningbo)
, known to the world as Master Yangming

Overjoyed at meeting his old friend, Wang Shouren hurriedly warmed a pot of wine and prepared a simple spread of dishes to welcome Gu Lin. After a couple of cups and some casual talk, the two gradually turned the conversation to the subject of learning. Gu Lin, smiling, pointed
at

Wang Shouren and said: “Since we parted in the capital so many years ago, I never imagined your learning would grow ever better and your fame ever greater — you have become a master of an age, worthy to be ranked with Lou Yizhai and Chen Xianzhang. It is a pity that all these years I have been trapped in officialdom, toiling and fretting day in and day out, with no time to study learning.”
Hearing this
Wang Shouren said at once: “Dongqiao

that is not right! What we call learning is in truth Confucius' practice of ‘subduing the self,’ and this practice can be carried out at any time and in any place. Especially for those in office, whose responsibilities are heavy

they must constantly judge right and wrong by their innate knowledge, and they must protect the good and cast out the bad; if they can regard the handling of public affairs as the practice of subduing the self
and carry it out earnestly, they will surely gain far more than ordinary people.”
Wang Shouren's words were quite novel, and Gu Lin asked with a smile: “How should a person in office pursue learning?

Wang Shouren thought for a moment. “You see, an official hearing a case is entangled in questions of right and wrong, straight and crooked; one word spoken amiss or one matter handled amiss can bring consequences too dreadful to contemplate. So officials must be not only just and incorruptible, but also calm and composed

They must not grow angry because a case is complicated, must not grow pleased because the plaintiff or defendant knows how to flatter, must not deliberately deal harshly with someone because the plaintiff or defendant has pulled strings behind the scenes, must not slight the law because the plaintiff or defendant pleads piteously for mercy, must not decide cases carelessly because they are busy, and must not, for fear that others will say their judgments are unfair, or in hope that the common folk will praise them as a ‘blue-sky magistrate,’ decide the case by going along
with

the opinion of the crowd. All of the above are selfish thoughts, and these selfish, distracting notions lie hidden in the official's heart where others cannot see them — only he himself knows of them. If this official can earnestly apply a round of effort to his innate knowledge and subdue these selfish and deviant thoughts, is this not the principle of ‘the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge’ spoken of in the Great Learning? What ‘things’ are investigated? They are his daily work and daily affairs
and what
knowledge’
is extended?
Naturally,
it
is the refining of one's innate knowledge.”

Wang Shouren spoke superbly! By the same reasoning, an official may refine his innate knowledge in handling public affairs; a merchant may refine his innate knowledge in buying and selling; a craftsman or artisan may refine his innate knowledge in plying his craft; a farmer may refine his innate knowledge in tilling his fields; and a student may refine his innate knowledge in studying his lessons. By the same reasoning, every person in the world can refine his innate knowledge at any time, in any place, and in any matter.
“So this is the state of ‘knowledge and
action united into
one’ that you always speak of?
Hearing Gu Lin's question, Wang Shouren answered frankly:
Knowledge and
action united as
one — that is how it should be.” Gu Lin laughed. “I have long heard people speak of your doctrine of ‘the unity of knowledge and action,’ but as I see it, this doctrine does not necessarily hold.”

All these years, as Wang Shouren had preached the way of “the unity of knowledge and action,” people had often come to debate him; now that Gu Lin said the same, Wang Shouren was not in the least surprised, and merely said with a smile: “Tell me, how does it not hold?
Gu Lin thought for a moment:

Let me ask: suppose there is a man who talks of ‘filial piety’ all day long, describing it in the most dazzling terms, yet when he returns home he does not at all serve his parents dutifully — such a man does exist, does he not? From this one matter alone we can see that ‘knowledge’ and ‘action’ are fundamentally two separate things. Don't you agree?
Gu Lin was a man of great talent, and his reasoning was something ordinary people could not refute.

But Wang Shouren, having passed through the enlightenment at Longchang and spent these years in diligent study and deep reflection, had thoroughly penetrated the four characters zhi xing he yi (“the unity of knowledge and action”), and no longer had any doubt. He said at once: “To the man you describe I would offer only eight characters: ‘To know and not to act is simply not yet to know.’”

These eight characters that Wang Shouren uttered were something he had slowly realized only through his own bitter seeking and much suffering. But Gu Lin had no such experience, and so had no way to understand them. He asked hastily:
What exactly do these eight characters mean?
Wang Shouren said with a smile: “When I speak of the unity of knowledge and action, this ‘knowledge’
is ‘innate knowledge’ (liangzhi)
and this ‘action’ is the practicing of innate knowledge. The example you just raised was that of ‘filial piety,’ and it is true that filial piety is a form of innate knowledge

As for the man you described, he always speaks of the word ‘filial piety,’ yet when he is truly before his parents he cannot serve them dutifully, because what his mouth says is not what his heart thinks

When this man tells others he is ‘filial,’ it is not that he wishes to serve his parents, but that he uses such words to deceive people, making others believe he is a filial son, gaining their respect and trust, and then reaping benefit from it. In truth, the innate knowledge of ‘filial piety’ has never arisen in him at all

Since the innate knowledge has not arisen, how can it be practiced? Naturally there is no action — this is what is called ‘knowing without acting.’ Why has the innate knowledge of ‘serving one's parents’ not arisen in this man's heart? Because filial piety is simply a ‘natural affection,’ and it happens that no natural affection for his parents has arisen in his heart. From the very root he does not know what ‘filial piety’ is — this is what is called ‘simply not yet knowing.’”
Wang Shouren's words made good sense, yet Gu Lin still had a doubt: “I can well believe that a man speaks of ‘filial piety’
while his heart holds no natural affection. But why would such a man be so at odds between word and heart? That is another strange thing.
Wang Shouren waved his hand. “Not strange at all! That a man's words and heart do not match, that his mouth says one thing and his heart another,

is only because his innate knowledge has been cut off by selfish desire and veiled by deviant thoughts. Do you suppose this man does not know at all what ‘filial piety’ is? Not so! In his heart he has innate knowledge, and he knows what ‘filial piety’ is; but his selfish desire and deviant
mind

are too strong, and the innate knowledge of ‘serving one's parents’ has been veiled by selfish desire, so that he ‘knows but cannot act.’ There are many such people, and it is not only a matter of ‘serving one's parents.’ For example, an official speaks of being incorruptible, yet underneath he is embezzling — it is not that he does not know he should be incorruptible, but that he is too weak and his deviant thoughts too strong, forcibly veiling the innate knowledge that he ‘ought to be incorruptible.’ A merchant speaks of being honest

yet underneath he is deceiving — it is not that he does not know the importance of honesty, but that his selfish desire is too strong, he is too fond of silver, and he has befuddled the innate knowledge that he ‘ought to be honest.’ Once innate knowledge is befuddled, in conducting oneself and handling affairs one's mouth will inevitably contradict one's heart, deceiving oneself and deceiving others. Seen in this light, ‘to know and not to act is simply not yet to know’ is truly a stubborn malady upon the people of the world — how many are sick to the marrow, yet still conceal their illness and refuse treatment!”
Once Wang Shouren

explained it in this way, Gu Lin understood; but at once another doubt arose: “Nowadays the world is foul, and greedy, corrupt people are everywhere. According to you, these people have all befuddled their own innate knowledge and let selfish desire run rampant, and only so have they fallen to this. I would ask you: if a person's conscience were never veiled, but pure and utterly pure, what would he be like?
This question of Gu Lin's was not easy to answer. Wang Shouren thought for a while before saying:

When a person's innate knowledge is unclouded, pure and utterly pure, then the moment a piece of innate knowledge arises in his heart he at once puts it into practice, without the least hesitation. To draw an analogy: when a person knows pain, it is because somewhere on his body there is pain

when he knows cold, it is because his body already feels cold; when he feels hunger, it is because he is already hungry. These pains, this cold, this hunger are all human instincts. In them there is no selfish desire cutting them off and no deviant thought veiling them, and so in these matters ‘the unity of knowledge and action’ is carried out most clearly and thoroughly. The moment he feels pain, he quickly dodges; the moment he feels cold, he quickly adds clothing; the moment he feels hungry, he quickly seeks something to eat
In these matters
every person can truly achieve ‘the unity of knowledge and action,’ and the two cannot be separated. Likewise, when a person knows filial piety, he must first have natural affection for his parents

when he knows fraternal respect, he must first have natural affection for his elder brother. Without natural affection for his parents, even a hundred repetitions of the word ‘filial piety’ are false; without natural affection for his elder brother, even a hundred repetitions of the word ‘fraternal respect’ are false. Therefore, the very moment we speak a single ‘knowledge,’ the content of ‘action’ is already within it
Knowledge is the beginning of action, and action is the completion of knowledge
knowledge is the guiding idea of action, and action is the effort of knowledge
and the two can never be separated. If a man's words and heart do not match — if his mouth speaks of ‘innate knowledge’ yet no action is seen in him

it shows that what his mouth speaks is false, and that the innate knowledge in his heart has in fact been veiled. Once innate knowledge is veiled, it becomes ‘not knowing’; without innate knowledge to guide him, practicing becomes ‘hard to practice,’ and both are ruined, amounting to nothing done at all. Tracing the root of the malady, it lies still in the veiling of innate knowledge. And so we say that such a man knows but does not act — he ‘simply has not found his innate knowledge.’”
Having heard these explanations, Gu Lin was wholly convinced. After a while he asked: “How is this malady of ‘knowing without acting’ to be cured?”

Wang Shouren said with a smile: “Once the root of the disease is found, the disease is easily cured. The root of ‘knowing without acting’ is that innate knowledge has been veiled by selfish desire; once you refine your innate knowledge out, the disease is cured.”

Gu Lin was a man of great talent and also a good official, and the innate knowledge in his heart had not been veiled very severely. Hearing this, he nodded repeatedly. Thinking again for a moment, he suddenly asked: “Since knowledge and action are in themselves one, why did the ancients then divide ‘knowledge’ and ‘action’ into two separate things to speak of?”

Wang Shouren paused a moment in reflection, then said: “As I see it, the ancients spoke in this way in order to save people. For in the world there is a kind of muddled, stubborn person who, in his confusion, knows only how to imagine things in empty speculation and will not put them into practice; for such a person one must lay stress on ‘action,’ urging him to go out and do things at once rather than sit at home in idle fancy. Then there is another kind of person, rash in the extreme, who never uses his head at all and only blunders about like a headless fly; for such a person one must stress the single word ‘knowledge,’ urging him to think deeply and carefully before acting, lest the moment he sets his hand to something he botch it. In the ancients' view, dividing ‘knowledge’ and ‘action’ into two matters was meant to urge the person who only seeks ‘knowledge’ without action to act more, and to urge the person who only buries his head in doing things without learning knowledge to use his head more
this is a method for curing the sick and saving people.
